```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 6, fig.height = 3.5)
r3 <- function(x) format(round(x, 3), nsmall = 3)
pct <- function(x) paste0(round(100 * x), "%")
mw <- function(d, e) format(round(d$ess$max_weight[d$ess$estimand == e], 2), nsmall = 2)
ess <- function(d, e, arm) format(round(d$ess[[paste0("ess_", arm)]][d$ess$estimand == e]))
lab <- function(e) c(ATE = "ATE", trimmed_ATE = "trimmed ATE", ATT = "ATT", ATO = "ATO")[[e]]
pop <- function(d, col, v) r3(d$populations[[col]][d$populations$covariate == v])
```

cleanTMLE runs an observational comparison in stages, so that the design is
settled before anyone sees the outcome. This is the clean-room idea of
@muntner2024staging. The package adds one question to the design stage:
can these data deliver the estimand we planned, and if not, which one can
they deliver?

In this vignette we take one simulated cohort through every stage. It takes
a few minutes to build. Each step says what it decides and what to look for
in its output.

## Why decide before seeing the outcome

Two problems motivate the stages. The first is analytic flexibility: when
the person choosing the model can see how each choice moves the estimate,
the final estimate carries those choices, however honest the person. The
second is positivity. An average treatment effect (ATE) needs every kind of
patient to have a real chance of either treatment. Where a group of
patients almost never receives one treatment, an estimator extrapolates,
and it can return a precise-looking estimate that is far from the truth
[@petersen2012positivity].

Keeping the outcome away from the design solves the first problem.
Checking, still without the outcome, which estimands the design can support
solves the second. The other estimands describe other populations: the
average treatment effect among the treated (ATT); the trimmed ATE, the
effect among patients whose propensity score lies inside a band
[@crump2009trimming]; and the overlap-weighted effect (ATO), which weights
each patient by how uncertain their treatment was [@li2018overlap]. In ICH
E9(R1) terms, moving between them changes the population attribute of the
estimand; the treatment, the outcome and the summary measure stay the same.

cleanTMLE estimates each of them with targeted maximum likelihood
estimation (TMLE), which combines a model for the outcome with a model for
the propensity score and stays consistent if either one is correct
[@vanderLaan2006tmle].

## The example cohort

`cr_example` is a simulated cohort of 1,500 patients. It comes as two
separate data frames, so that the outcome stays out of the design stage.

```{r data}
library(cleanTMLE)
str(cr_example$design)
str(cr_example$outcomes)
```

The question is the effect of treatment `A` on death within 30 days
(`death_30d`), measured as a risk difference: the difference in the
proportion of patients who die within 30 days. A risk difference describes
the whole target population directly and, unlike a hazard ratio from a Cox
model, does not depend on a proportional-hazards assumption. Treatment
depends strongly on `severity`, so few severe patients go untreated and few
mild patients are treated. Because the data are simulated, we know the true
effect for each estimand; it is in `cr_example$truth`, and we compare our
estimate with it at the end.

## Step 1: declare the plan

Everything about the analysis is set once, in the plan. Nothing can be
added after the next step.

```{r plan}
plan <- analysis_plan(
  outcome = "death_30d",
  estimands = c("ATE", "trimmed_ATE", "ATT", "ATO"),
  trim_band = c(0.05, 0.95),
  ps_library = "glm",
  candidates = list(library = list(glm = "glm"), truncation = 0.01),
  surfaces = list(forms = "linear"),
  negative_controls = c(health_seeking = "health care use"),
  restrictions = list(no_transfer = ~ transfer == 0),
  roles = list(analyst = "A. Analyst", reviewers = "Review team"),
  K = 1, reps = 50, max_reps = 50, seed = 1)
```

The `estimands` are a ladder, in order of preference: the first one the
design can support becomes the primary estimand. `trim_band` defines the
trimmed population. `ps_library` is the model for the propensity score, and
`candidates` lists the outcome models and the truncation levels to compare.
Truncation bounds the estimated propensity score, here at 0.01 and 0.99,
inside the estimator; it limits extreme weights without removing anyone.
Trimming, by contrast, removes the patients outside the band from the
target population. `surfaces` describes the simulated outcomes the design
stage tests against (step 4). `negative_controls` names an outcome that
treatment should not affect, and `restrictions` lists cohort restrictions
to check it under.

The plan also holds defaults we did not change. An estimand is accepted
when, in the simulation, its estimator's absolute bias is at most
`r plan$tolerance$bias` on the risk difference scale and the coverage of
its 95% confidence interval is at least `r plan$tolerance$coverage`. The
negative control passes when its interval lies within
`r plan$nc_criteria$null_band[1]` to `r plan$nc_criteria$null_band[2]`.

This plan is deliberately small so that the vignette builds in a few
minutes: logistic regression only, no cross-fitting (`K = 1`), and 50
simulated repetitions. A real analysis keeps the defaults. These are a
super learner, which combines several machine-learning models by
cross-validation, with one learner of each kind; five-fold cross-fitting,
which fits the models on part of the data and predicts on the rest; and
200 or more repetitions. The vignette "Writing the plan and reading the
dossier" explains each choice.

## Step 2: lock the design data

```{r lock}
lock <- create_analysis_lock(cr_example$design, treatment = "A",
                             covariates = c("age", "female", "severity", "prior_visits"),
                             plan = plan)
```

The lock holds the plan and the design data, and refuses data that contain
the outcome column. Its hash is a fingerprint of both:

```{r hash}
substr(lock$lock_hash, 1, 16)
```

If the plan or the design data change after this point, the hash no longer
matches and every later step stops. The lock cannot stop anyone from
analyzing the outcome outside the package; what it guarantees is that any
change to the plan or the design data is detectable. The outcome enters
the package only at step 6.

## Step 3: assess the design

```{r design}
design <- assess_design(lock)
design
```

The overlap grade is `r design$overlap_grade`: `r pct(design$share_outside_band)`
of patients have an estimated propensity score outside the trim band (the
grade is good below 5%, moderate below 20%, and poor otherwise). The
c-statistic of the propensity score is `r r3(design$c_statistic)`; values
near 1 mean treatment is close to predictable from the covariates.

The table gives, for each estimand, the effective sample size in each arm,
the largest weight, and the 99th percentile of the weights. For the ATE the
largest weight is `r mw(design, "ATE")`: one patient counts as that many
patients who look like them but received the other treatment. The ATT
needs controls who look like the treated, and the effective number of
controls for it is only `r ess(design, "ATT", "control")`. Overlap weights
are at most 1, so for the ATO the largest weight is `r mw(design, "ATO")`.

The plot shows why. Near a propensity score of 0 almost every patient is a
control, and near 1 most are treated.

```{r design-plot}
plot(design)
```

Changing the estimand changes the population the answer is about. The
`populations` table gives, for each estimand, the mean of each covariate
in its target population and the standardized mean difference from the
full cohort (the columns ending in `_shift`):

```{r populations}
design$populations[, c("covariate", "cohort", "trimmed_ATE", "ATT", "ATO",
                       "trimmed_ATE_shift", "ATT_shift", "ATO_shift")]
```

Severity shows the difference. Its mean is `r pop(design, "cohort", "severity")`
in the cohort and `r pop(design, "ATT", "severity")` among the treated, a
standardized mean difference of `r pop(design, "ATT_shift", "severity")`. The
trimmed and overlap-weighted populations differ from the cohort by
`r pop(design, "trimmed_ATE_shift", "severity")` and
`r pop(design, "ATO_shift", "severity")`. An answer about the treated is an
answer about sicker patients.

The trimmed population leaves out the patients outside the band. Here is
who they are:

```{r trimmed}
design$trimmed_profile$counts
design$trimmed_profile$covariates
```

When fewer than five patients are removed or kept, these means are not
shown, so that the dossier never reports values for one or two
individuals.

## Step 4: test the design with simulated outcomes

The outcome is still locked away. To learn which estimands the design can
deliver, `simulate_design()` runs a plasmode simulation: it keeps the real
covariates, draws new treatments from the estimated propensity score, and
draws outcomes from a family of outcome models fixed in the plan, which
the package calls outcome surfaces. Because it built those outcomes, it
knows the true effect in each simulated dataset, so it can check whether
each estimator recovers it. Drawing new treatments, rather than keeping
each patient's observed one, matters: keeping them builds a positivity
violation into the simulation [@shaw2025plasmode].

```{r simulate}
sim <- simulate_design(lock, design)
sim$verdict[, c("estimand", "status", "selected", "ci_halfwidth", "unresolved")]
```

An estimand is feasible when an estimator meets the bias and coverage
tolerances on every surface. Here the ATE is
`r sim$verdict$status[sim$verdict$estimand == "ATE"]` and the trimmed ATE
is `r sim$verdict$status[sim$verdict$estimand == "trimmed_ATE"]`, so the
ladder moves one rung down. `selected` names the chosen candidate: the
outcome model (`glm`) and the truncation level (`t0.01`). `ci_halfwidth`
is the expected half-width of the 95% confidence interval, which tells you,
before seeing any outcome, how precise the answer will be.

Each check is itself an estimate from a finite number of simulated
datasets. `unresolved` is `TRUE` when that uncertainty is too large to say
whether a tolerance was met. With only 50 repetitions,
`r if (all(sim$verdict$unresolved)) "every check here is unresolved" else "some checks here are unresolved"`; a real analysis uses more repetitions and lets `max_reps` add
them where they could change the decision.

## Step 5: check a negative control

`health_seeking` records health care use that treatment should not affect.
If adjustment removes confounding, its estimated effect should be near
zero.

```{r nc}
nc <- negative_control_ladder(lock, design, sim)
nc$by_rung
```

The control is estimated for every estimand, first on the full cohort and
then under each restriction; the `rung` column says which. Each estimand's
control is fitted with the candidate the simulation selected for that
estimand, so the check tests the adjustment the analysis will use (the
`candidate` column of `nc$table` names it). For an estimand the simulation found
infeasible, which has no selected candidate, the control uses the candidate
with the smallest worst-case error in the simulation, and
`candidate_feasible` is `FALSE`. Here the
restriction excludes patients transferred in from another hospital, who may
differ in ways the covariates do not capture. For each estimand the verdict
is GO when every control's 95% interval lies inside the null band, STOP
when any lies entirely outside it, and FLAG otherwise. Only the full-cohort
verdict for the estimand the analysis will report can block unblinding.
Estimands the design cannot deliver can read STOP for a reason other than
confounding: a control read on such an estimand mixes extrapolation error
with confounding.

## Step 6: build the dossier and unblind

The dossier collects the decision and everything behind it, and
fingerprints them.

```{r dossier}
dossier <- design_report(lock, design, sim, nc)
dossier
```

```{r nc-row, include = FALSE}
nc_row <- subset(nc$table, rung == "full cohort" & estimand == dossier$decision$primary)
```

The primary estimand is the `r lab(dossier$decision$primary)`, and the
negative-control verdict for it is `r dossier$decision$nc_verdict`. On that
estimand the control's interval runs from `r r3(nc_row$ci_lower)` to
`r r3(nc_row$ci_upper)`, much wider than the null band, so the check cannot
rule out residual confounding as large as the band. FLAG does not block
unblinding; the dossier reports it for the review team.

The rendered dossier, `design_report(..., file = "dossier.html")`, also
shows the plan, the population tables, the full simulation results, and the
expected number of events in each arm, computed from the outcome surfaces
and the observed treatment without reading the outcome:

```{r events}
ev <- dossier$expected_events_range
ev[-1] <- round(ev[-1])
ev
```

The ATE, ATT and ATO use every patient, so their rows match; the trimmed
ATE uses only the patients inside the band. The range comes from the
different outcome surfaces, and the treatment effect changes only the
treated arm.

In a real study the review team reads the rendered dossier before
approving. Here `r if (all(sim$verdict$unresolved)) "every check is" else "some checks are"`
unresolved, so a review team should ask for more repetitions before approving. We approve only to show the next step:

```{r unblind}
ub <- unblind(lock, dossier, cr_example$outcomes, approved_by = "Review team")
```

`unblind()` checks that the dossier belongs to this lock and has not been
changed before it admits the outcome.

## Step 7: estimate the effect

```{r estimate}
fit <- estimate_effect(ub)
fit
truth <- cr_example$truth$truth[cr_example$truth$estimand == fit$estimand]
```

`estimate_effect()` uses the estimand and the candidate the dossier
selected. The estimated `r lab(fit$estimand)`, a difference in 30-day risk,
is `r r3(fit$estimate)` (95% CI: `r r3(fit$ci_lower)`, `r r3(fit$ci_upper)`),
and the true value in this simulated cohort is `r r3(truth)`, which the
interval
`r if (fit$ci_lower <= truth && truth <= fit$ci_upper) "contains" else "does not contain"`.
The true value is computed over the patients whose true propensity score
lies in the band, while the estimate trims on the estimated score, so the
two populations are close but not identical (see `?cr_example`).

A weighting estimator gives a comparison on the same estimand. It was not
tested in the design stage, and the result says so:

```{r weighting}
estimate_effect(ub, method = "weighting")
```

## Step 8: export the record

The design log records every decision, who made it, and the hashes that tie
it together. The `"muntner"` format gives the columns of the decision log in
@muntner2024staging.

```{r log}
log <- export_design_log(ub, fit, format = "muntner")
log[, c("stage", "issue", "decision", "decided_by")]
```
